1b9aba616b.q: How does pulsar-based localization work for spacecraft navigation at relativistic speeds?
1b9aba616b.a: Pulsars pulse at relatively unique and identifiable frequencies, allowing localization within a certain range. If you observe multiple pulsars and know their cosmological positions, you can identify your location. f: Pulsars pulse at relatively unique and identifiable frequencies, allowing localization within a certain range. If you observe multiple pulsars and know their cosmological positions, you can identify your location. However, optical resolution limits (the Rayleigh limit) constrain accuracy to roughly plus or minus a million kilometers in any direction. At relativistic speeds, you must account for both special and general relativity, Doppler shifts, and the vectors of moving stars to achieve accuracy. Dead reckoning combined with pulsar tracking—knowing your speed, heading, and initial position—can narrow localization to usable frames of reference of possibly meters over time.
1b9aba616b.rq: Localization is the real problem because that, in robotics, whatever problem you want to work on is the hardest problem.
ks: Localization accuracy with four pulsars: plus or minus one million kilometers in any direction due to Rayleigh diffraction limits
Orientation accuracy with pulsar tracking: roughly one thousandth of a degree
GPS/GNSS accuracy for position: plus or minus 30 meters for cheap dash cameras, despite speed discrimination being highly accurate
Travel time to nearest star at speed of light: approximately four years; at 20% speed of light: roughly 20 years
Kilohertz range: pulsar brightness changes occur at kilohertz frequencies, requiring fast camera sensors

73b065e833.q: Why is localization harder than other robotics problems even in advanced sci-fi scenarios?
73b065e833.a: In robotics, whatever problem you want to work on ends up being the hardest problem, and localization consistently remains unsolved. Even in futuristic scenarios where force fields, relativistic travel, and advanced AI exist, localization breaks down. People claiming localization is a solved problem are still wrong. The reason is that finding your absolute position accurately requires measuring against fixed reference points, and the physics—especially optics and the Rayleigh limit—fundamentally constrains what is achievable. f: In robotics, whatever problem you want to work on ends up being the hardest problem, and localization consistently remains unsolved. Even in futuristic scenarios where force fields, relativistic travel, and advanced AI exist, localization breaks down. People claiming localization is a solved problem are still wrong. The reason is that finding your absolute position accurately requires measuring against fixed reference points, and the physics—especially optics and the Rayleigh limit—fundamentally constrains what is achievable. Networking also fails to help; even with intelligent systems, communication breakdowns mean robots cannot share location data reliably.
